paras: The killing of Brooks and Griffey was the shooting of two prisoners in James County, Tennessee, in January 1881, held on suspicion of murdering a farmer, Henry Yarnell. Rifle shots fired at night into the shop where they were held killed both men, and a widely reprinted dispatch blamed friends of Yarnell. In June 1881 a grand jury indicted three of the men who had guarded them, all relatives of Yarnell, but no report of a trial was found.

Someone set fire to a hay rick belonging to Yarnell in a county adjoining Chattanooga's, according to the Courier-Journal's Chattanooga correspondent. While searching for the incendiaries with a man named Howe, Yarnell was shot through the brain and Howe was badly wounded in the mouth. A Memphis Appeal note placed the shooting in Yarnell's own yard in James County, by "a concealed assassin," and called the wounded man "Mr. Lowe." The dispatch found no proof of a motive but believed the shooting grew out of "an old feud."

Several men were arrested the next day; the Ooltewah correspondent of the Cleveland Weekly Herald listed Elijah Brooks, "sometimes called Myers," Griffey, George Irwin, Dr. Priddy, two others and "a colored man named Howard." Irwin and Howard were released and Priddy bonded, but Brooks and Griffey were kept under guard. Being some distance from a jail, the two were confined in a blacksmith shop guarded by two men, according to the wire; the Herald described "a little shoe shop" guarded principally by William Norman.

During the night a noise was heard at the windows and two rifles fired almost at once, killing both prisoners instantly with shots to the head. The Herald placed the shooting on the Tuesday night after Yarnell was killed on a Sunday night, with the shots supposedly fired through cracks in the building. Amid "the greatest excitement," several men were arrested and moved to another part of the county for fear of lynching.

At the first term of court after the killings, the grand jury indicted Dr. Priddy, whose case was continued under bond. A later term indicted Francis Norman, his son William Norman and Samuel Maddox, whom Sheriff Clingan and a posse arrested at their homes in early June. According to the Knoxville Chronicle, the Normans were physicians, Yarnell had been their brother-in-law and Maddox's uncle, and the three had been guarding the prisoners. It reported the allegation that they killed the prisoners, blamed unknown parties, and so avenged their kinsman.

On a writ of habeas corpus, Judge Trewhitt at Ooltewah admitted the three to bail of $5,000 and ordered them to reappear on June 25. In January 1882 the Chattanooga Times reported a nolle prosequi in Priddy's case after the proof became "less positive." No report of a trial of the Normans or Maddox was found.

The first account, a Chattanooga special to the Courier-Journal relayed from Louisville on January 22, ran within two days from Yankton, Dakota Territory, to Chicago and Savannah. Headlines treated it as crime news: "In Cold Blood" in the Memphis Public Ledger, "Incendiarism and Murder" in the Savannah Morning News, and "Two Murders in Return Shot by Unknown Parties" in the Wheeling Register. The St. Paul Daily Globe filed it under "Shooting and Lynching," the Omaha Bee as "Swift Retribution," and the New-York Tribune, following the Louisville dateline, as "A Double Tragedy in Kentucky."

Weekly digests described a tragedy in which "three, perhaps four, men lost their lives," and Tennessee weeklies reprinted the wire without comment. The Rock Island Argus added "(white)" after Yarnell's name; no paper stated the race of Brooks or Griffey.

In June the Knoxville Chronicle, while reporting the revenge charge, called the accused "men of high standing and respectability." The Herald's Ooltewah correspondent complained that the Chattanooga Times had done them "great injustice" by appearing to "find them guilty" before trial, and called the case "mere conjecture."

The January dispatch blamed unknown persons outside the shop, believed to be Yarnell's friends, while the June reports named the guards themselves as the accused. Details also vary: a blacksmith's or a shoemaker's shop, two guards or three, and in one Memphis brief a victim named "Banks" and a May date for Yarnell's death.

reader.title: Killing of Brooks and Griffey
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Two men held under guard as suspects in a murder were shot dead in custody by gunmen the wire believed to be the murdered man's friends, and a grand jury later indicted their guards, kinsmen of the dead man (A2, A32, A34).

Both prisoners were shot dead while under arrest on suspicion of Yarnell's murder, and the wire attributed the killing to Yarnell's friends while the Knoxville Chronicle alleged that his three kinsmen guarding them did it in revenge (A2, A32). Two rifles were fired and three men were indicted, but no report fixes how many took part (A2, A34).

The Courier-Journal wire (A2) and separate Tennessee reports from Ooltewah and Knoxville (A34, A32) agree that Brooks and Griffey were shot dead while under guard as suspects in Yarnell's murder; they disagree on who fired.

accounts.gist: The prisoners were shot through cracks in a shoe shop while guarded principally by William Norman; who fired remained a mystery, and the correspondent defended the indicted men against prejudgment.

accounts.label: Knoxville Chronicle
accounts.gist: The three guards, Yarnell's kinsmen, were accused of killing their prisoners and claiming unknown parties had shot them, to avenge Yarnell.

framing.detail: Papers from Yankton to Savannah reprinted the Courier-Journal special under crime headlines such as 'In Cold Blood' and 'Incendiarism and Murder'.
The St. Paul Daily Globe headed it 'Shooting and Lynching'; the Omaha Bee ran it as 'Swift Retribution' among 'Village Fueds'.
In June the Knoxville Chronicle reported the revenge allegation but called the accused 'men of high standing and respectability'.
The Herald's Ooltewah correspondent faulted the Chattanooga Times for prejudging the accused and called the case 'mere conjecture'.

versions.value: Unknown persons outside the shop, believed friends of Yarnell
The guards themselves, Yarnell's kin, accused and indicted

conflicts.note: The June reports are later and local and rest on indictments, but they report an accusation, not a finding.
The Ooltewah correspondent is local; the wire is from Chattanooga.
'Geo. Jeffry' in the Omaha Bee is OCR garble of Griffey.
Every other report, including the wire of January 22, puts the killings in January.

record_check.dossier: Louisville is only the relay dateline of the Courier-Journal special; the killing took place in James County, near Ooltewah, in a county adjoining Chattanooga's.

record_check.record: Geo. Jeffry, Brooks, Griffey, Gritiey, Grifey
record_check.dossier: Two victims: Elijah Brooks (also called Myers) and Griffey; the other names are OCR variants.
Race not stated in any report; the only man called 'colored' (Howard) was arrested and released. Should be unknown, not 2.
Wire: unknown, believed friends of Yarnell; later the guards Francis Norman, William Norman and Samuel Maddox, Yarnell's kin, were indicted.
No mob or crowd is described; two riflemen fired at night, and the accused were the guards.
Mid-January 1881, the Tuesday night after Yarnell was shot on a Sunday night; before the wire of January 21-22.

info: Mid-January 1881: Yarnell was shot on a Sunday night and the prisoners on the following Tuesday night; the wire of Jan. 21-22 says 'a few nights ago'.
A shop where the prisoners were held: a blacksmith shop (wire) or 'a little shoe shop' (Ooltewah correspondent), in a county adjoining Chattanooga's.
Elijah Brooks, 'sometimes called Myers', and a man named Griffey (OCR variants Griley, Griirey, Jeffry; 'Banks' for Brooks in one brief).
Arrested on suspicion of shooting Henry Yarnell, a farmer, and wounding a man named Howe (or Lowe).

Wire: unknown persons firing from outside, believed to be friends of Yarnell. June reports: the guards, Francis (or Frank, or Vance) Norman, his son William Norman and Samuel Maddox (Mattox), Yarnell's kinsmen, were indicted and accused.
Not stated; no paper gives the race of Brooks or Griffey.
Nolle prosequi entered in Dr. Priddy's case (suspected in Yarnell's murder) at Ooltewah in January 1882; no outcome found for the Normans and Maddox.
